title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
description: Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcemen
body: Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.A representative of the DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was put online on Wednesday by a group called the Department of Peace alongside cybersecurity researcher and hacker maia crimew.The information was put in a database named Icepick and shared through a website hosted by Distributed Denial of Secrets.Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE. Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.   The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets."The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in it's simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the groups work to hack DHS records. "On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security. The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents. In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt. Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, external, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people. Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded, external DHS enforces the requirement. Since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the US has enacted nearly 1 million deportations, external, according to data from the Migration Policy Institute. More than 70% of the deportations have been of people with no criminal record.

schema.headline: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack

title: Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite range of small measures
description: This was a Budget I would describe as a flotilla of small measures.Westminster is poring over the 150 page Red Book, external in which the Budget is p
body: This was a Budget I would describe as a flotilla of small measures.Westminster is poring over the 150 page Red Book, external in which the Budget is printed and also what is formally called the Economic and Fiscal Outlook published, external by the watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility, the OBR.The Red Book sets out the measures the chancellor will implement and how much they will cost. There are 98 of them, considerably more than normal and more than in either of Rachel Reeves' budgets.But nearly all of them are pretty small in terms of their impact on the Treasury's spreadsheets.This gets to the heart of why those involved in compiling this Budget have been irritated by commentary in the build up to it suggesting there would be nothing to see in John Healey's address – but also why those suggesting that were arguably onto something as well.Firstly, as expected, it was a much smaller Budget in overall tax and spending terms than plenty of recent ones have been. But there were plenty of measures here and there which the chancellor will hope enough people notice and value – and others that some will likely curse.There are more taxes for savers and landlords, for instance, and too for banks.When a government has promised, as Labour have, to not put up income tax, national insurance or VAT – the big revenue generators – they end up looking elsewhere if they conclude putting up tax is necessary. That runs the political risk of choosing particular sectors who might respond rather noisily. Think of the plenty of farmers who were incensed by the changes to inheritance tax Rachel Reeves was keen on.The central challenge for Healey, which he shares with his recent predecessors, is the public finances are in a mess and so are the personal finances of so, so many households. And there is a recurring sense of déjà vu in the language of the OBR. "The UK's economic and fiscal position remains very challenging," it says, with a splash of understatement, adding that "there have been further adverse developments" this year with in the conflict in the Middle East.As for what happens, next, well, frankly, who on earth knows. Or, as the OBR puts it: "The outlook for the economy and the public finances is uncertain, with significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability."The Budget book argues that "the UK economy is showing signs of resilience" but it is also true that the national debt, tax burden, inflation and interest rates are high, going up or both – and there could yet be further economic shocks that make things worse.What happens, for instance, in the Middle East, once the mid term elections are done in America and the result of the Israeli general election is clear?In short, the chancellor felt constrained in his capacity to act and his capacity to make a noticeable positive difference is perhaps constrained even more so – because any intervention, even expensive ones, may merely make a grim situation a bit less bad, rather than things actually feeling better. Mitigating the bad is arguably a noble political aim, but it costs money and potentially comes with little political upside.Instead there is this fleet of smaller measures that the government will hope gives their MPs something to try to sell – while acknowledging that they are not world changing.Luke Tryl, the UK Director of the More in Common think tank, says: "The softly populist tone of this budget is likely to land well with the public. The Chancellor targeted groups the public have little sympathy with - banks, landlords, gambling companies and vape shops - and turned it into cost-of-living support, rate relief for small businesses and ensuring the state pension isn't taxed."He adds: "Crucially, the chancellor may have avoided the biggest potential trap of the Budget - being seen to offer energy support for those on benefits and incurring the ire of the squeezed middle, who think they work hard but are left to fend for themselves. "Instead, by offering support to all of those on Council Tax bands A to D, he is able to reassure them that the government will support them too."The reaction of the opposition parties, from a range of different political perspectives, amounts to a critique that this Budget was thin. The government counters that it is one piece in the emerging jigsaw of detail from the new-ish prime minister and his chancellor – with a plan help young people into work and cut benefits before Christmas, alongside a big picture sense of what the UK's long term relationship with the European Union could look like and a 10 year vision from Andy Burnham.In summary, this felt like a cautious Budget. One critical friend of the government suggested to me this would be a "Mr Sensible Budget" – their hope and expectation that it might be shorn of bells and whistles, but shorn of timebombs too. Let's see.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite range of small measures

title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
description: The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.The Heroe
body: The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, at the age of 36.Citing the medical examiner's report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had "concluded its investigation" into her death.The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment."Based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental," police said in a statement.Authorities, including the DEA, were reportedly investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

schema.headline: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe

title: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
description: Protecting this region from climate change is a theme of the King's trip and was the focus of his visit to the Bonefish Pond National Park. The site w
body: Protecting this region from climate change is a theme of the King's trip and was the focus of his visit to the Bonefish Pond National Park. The site was once a rubbish dump but has been redeveloped and now protects 1,235 acres of mangroves.The King walked along a new boardwalk through the wetlands to see the conservation work being done to protect this vulnerable, low lying island from climate change.He met students carrying out field work in the wetland waters asking them about their exams and ambitions to be marine biologists."We've so been looking forward to this," said Joanne Smith, President of the Bahamas National Trust Council."We want more Bahamians to get involved in our national parks so they can use it to better themselves… we are so pleased to have the King here, this is really significant for us."Then it was on to the Junkanoo, where the King could be seen dancing alongside attendees dressed in feathered headdresses and bright costumes. The history of the Junkanoo is not clear but it's believed it emerged out of the slave trade when enslaved men and women were given time off to mark Christmas.A small protest near the parade was moved on by the police.The King ended his day with a garden reception at Government House in Nassau where he met Bahamians who have made significant contributions to public life.In a speech, Dame Cynthia A Pratt, the governor general of the Bahamas who is the King's representative on the island, described her pride at Charles visiting the country for the first time since 1973."We trust that your time in our capital will reflect the legendary hospitality of our people," said Dame Cynthia."We pray that this royal visit further strengthens the enduring bonds of friendship between the Crown and the Bahamian people."On Thursday, the Caribbean tour leaves the Bahamas as the King continues his visit in Guyana.The trip has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.The King will move to Guyana later this week where his engagements will focus on the environment and biodiversity.He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

schema.headline: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour

title: Russell Brand tells trial sexual consent is 'fundamental'
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentRussell Brand has told the jury at his trial he believes sexual consent is "fundamental" and "more impor
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentRussell Brand has told the jury at his trial he believes sexual consent is "fundamental" and "more important than sex itself". Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of attempted indecent assault.The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.Giving evidence on Wednesday, Brand said the allegations had been "deeply traumatic" and had a "devastating" impact on him.The media personality gave evidence as his defence case began at his trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.Asked whether consent was important to him, he told the court: "Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself."Brand told the court he had previously been "comfortable" allowing his fame to "facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong".But asked by the prosecution whether he "needed and was prepared to go to any lengths", Brand replied: "Absolutely no."Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC suggested to Brand there were inconsistencies between his previous prepared police statement and what he told the jury."Ms Karmy-Jones, I completely agree," he replied. "Since these events occurred there's been escalating recollection."It's been a deeply traumatic episode of my life. I've focused on it at the expense of my marriage, my children and health."I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that."He said: "I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man."With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I've been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy."He told the jury: "Regrettably I've had a lot of consensual sex, which I see has caused harm."After Brand entered the witness box on Wednesday morning, defence barrister Ian Winter KC began by taking him through the indictment, asking him if he had committed the offences.After each question, Brand replied "no" loudly towards the jury.Brand was then asked about the Channel 4 documentary and the impact it had on his relationships with friends and colleagues. "It was devastating," Brand said.Winter questioned whether Brand had been able to persuade any friend or acquaintance who might have been able to give evidence on his behalf to appear in court.Brand replied: "I have not." Winter asked: "Will they touch you with a bargepole?" Brand said: "No."Brand also claimed in court that he was told he could not stay with his son at Great Ormond Street hospital in London when the child was having open heart surgery, following the documentary and a newspaper investigation.He told the court: "Due to material that had been published in the public eye they had to bar my attendance and presence."Brand told the court: "My entire life has been consumed by these allegations," adding that he had "devoted myself to these matters".Winter asked Brand if he recalled meeting the first complainant, who alleges he raped her at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.Brand said yes, explaining that he found her "loquacious" and "interesting".When asked if there was any truth in the allegations that he raped her, he said: "No."Under cross examination, the prosecution suggested Brand "just didn't care whether she was interested in having sex with you or not". Brand rejected that, saying he did care "very much".Asked whether he was sure he "didn't think no means yes", he replied: "I know what no means."Brand was then asked about another woman, who alleges that the entertainer grabbed her breasts before dragging her into a toilet and raping her.Brand said he recalled been invited to a party in London at a bar in 2004, and said a friend had introduced him to the complainant by saying "something like 'there's a bird here who really wants to meet you mate'."When asked if he remembered what he said to her upon meeting, he told the court: "I would have said something like, 'You're really, really beautiful'."The barrister asked whether he had grabbed her breasts. "Absolutely not," Brand replied.When questioned if he would have behaved in the way that had been alleged, he said it would have amounted to "disgusting behaviour"."I was increasingly focused on my promiscuity," he said. "That's not the way I would have behaved because it's not only criminal but vulgar."Brand said he remembered going into the toilet with her but said "no" when asked if he had dragged or forced her there."Did your penis enter her mouth at all whilst in the cubicle?" Winter asked. "No," said Brand.Another complainant, who worked at MTV, alleges that Brand tried to drag her into a toilet at work in 2001.At the time, he was one of the channel's star presenters. She said she managed to wrench herself away.Asked if he had intended a non-consensual sexual encounter, Brand told the court: "Absolutely not."In relation to another woman, who accuses Brand of anal rape, he said he remembered her being in his dressing room at the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London in 2009 after his comedy show.He said after a "memorable" sexual encounter, he contacted her again to try to meet, adding: "I was excited and enthusiastic about it."Brand also said he had saved her number in his phone using a code, saying: "That was what I used to denote casual hook-ups and women I met I could hook up with."After inviting her to his house in Hampstead, he said they had consensual sex in his room.When asked if he committed anal rape, he said no. When asked if she had asked him to stop, he said no.Asked by the prosecution later if his memory was "a little selective" in what he could remember, Brand replied: "No."Brand was also asked on Wednesday about his wedding to singer Katy Perry in October 2010 and whether it brought a "sea change" to his life. He said the marriage brought him "staggering fame".Being cross examined, Brand agreed with the prosecution's suggestion that he blamed Channel 4 documentary programme Dispatches for the allegations.Asked if the media had been fair to him, Brand said he "would reject that suggestion strongly". Under intense questioning from Karmy-Jones, Brand denied pretending to be gay in his pursuit of women, after one of the complainants said they assumed he was gay and that she had felt "sexually safe with him".Brand also told the jury he had an obsession with sex as a younger man but denied giving himself a "goal" to sleep with 5,000 women.From the witness box, he said consent was "non-negotiable".The trial continues.

schema.headline: Russell Brand tells trial sexual consent is 'fundamental'

title: What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out
description: If you are an 18-to-20 year-old earning the minimum wage, your pay will go up by 3.9% from next April.However, the increase may be lower than you had
body: If you are an 18-to-20 year-old earning the minimum wage, your pay will go up by 3.9% from next April.However, the increase may be lower than you had expected. That is because Healey reversed course on how his Labour predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had been increasing the minimum wage for young people. Labour had promised to do away with "discriminatory age bands", with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage. This year, 18-20 year-olds will see the same increase as older workers, meaning the disparity will remain. So, for 18-to-20 year-olds, your pay will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.The increase also means a 21-year-old, who is working full time on the minimum wage and took out a student loan after 2023, will now earn enough to meet the £25,000 repayment threshold, over which they will start paying back 9% of their earnings.The Budget contained plans to help people get onto the housing ladder, including the introduction of a "First Time Buyer Isa". This is an account in which savers can build up a deposit, with the government topping up contributions of up to £4,000 each year with a 25% bonus. The new savings account will be introduced in 2029, replacing the existing Lifetime Isa, which has been criticised by some for imposing harsh penalties on those buying homes for more than the £450,000 cap. The cap will remain, but the new "First Time Buyer Isa" will ensure savers are not penalised by losing their own money when making withdrawals. Savers will only lose contributions made by the government when making withdrawals which are not eligible for the account.The penalty for withdrawals from existing Lifetime Isas will be lowered, too, to address concerns about savers being punished.  The government had already revealed a £4.7bn scheme for first-time buyers in England dubbed Your First Home. It is aiming to help 70,000 individuals and couples get on the housing ladderThe scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It will provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.Capped at £110,000 outside London and £140,000 in the capital, it is aimed at those hoping to get on the housing ladder without help from "the bank of mum and dad".

schema.headline: What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out

title: John Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
description: Image source, Press AssociationByBrian WheelerPolitical reporterUpdated 4 hours agoMillions of households will get £100 to help with soaring energy bi
body: Image source, Press AssociationByBrian WheelerPolitical reporterUpdated 4 hours agoMillions of households will get £100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, John Healey has announced in his first Budget.The chancellor said he wanted to give hard-pressed families "breathing space now" and "hope for the future" as the UK economy is battered by "global economic storms".He also unveiled tax breaks to boost high street businesses - but confirmed that many big decisions, including on defence spending and welfare, will not be made until next year.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Healey's plans were "not bold enough" and the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".In an hour-long speech to a packed House of Commons, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other frontbench colleagues cheering him on, the chancellor unveiled a string of measures aimed at cutting the cost of living.These include: One-off £100 energy payment for people living in council tax bands A to D in England, with Wales saying it will match the payment and the Scottish government planning to "replicate" itGas standing charges in England, Scotland and Wales, to be scrapped during 2027 "or as soon as possible after". These fixed daily fees will be shifted onto the price of each unit of energy, meaning heavy gas users will face higher billsExtending the 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel to JulyIncreasing minimum wage rates by 3.9% in April, although there will be no progress on narrowing the gap between rates for older and younger workersHealey increased the tax on the profits of big banks from 3% to 6%, which will last from January next year to April 2028, and increased taxes on high-stakes gambling machines.As part of a package to help business, Healey increased the point at which High Street shops in England start paying business rates from £12,000 to £18,000, with vape shops and adult gaming centres excluded from the relief.But he had little scope for big giveaways as the public finances remain stretched, with the UK set to spend £14bn more on debt interest payments this year.Income tax thresholds will remain frozen and the tax on income from savings and property rental will rise to 24% for basic rate taxpayers from April 2027, after it had been scheduled to go up to 22%.But a cut to the cash ISA allowance from £20,000 a year to £12,000, announced last year by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, will be axed.The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded its growth forecast for next year to 1%, with slightly higher increases predicted for subsequent years.In its latest assessment, the OBR said British households were set to be little better off than before the Covid pandemic even a decade after Covid-19 hit, a situation the watchdog's boss David Miles described as "pretty grim".In his Budget speech, Healey repeatedly stressed that the UK economy was being battered by "global uncertainties" and soaring oil prices caused by conflict in the Middle East. "Those are the storms we face. We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them," he told MPs.Figure caption, Watch: What are the key points from the Budget and how will it be funded?Healey also used his speech to announce plans to allow regional mayors to keep 20% of business rates and a share of income tax to spend on local priorities.The aim was to allow mayors to retain 100% of business rates raised in their areas by the end of the decade, he added, in "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".And he sought to address opposition claims the Labour government is unwilling to cut benefits, insisting that both he and Burnham were committed to bringing down the welfare bill in a "Labour way".But he said no decisions would be taken until reviews by Alan Milburn, into young people not in work or training, and Stephen Timms, on Personal Independence Payments, had been published, with legislation to follow next year.The £4.7bn black hole in the defence investment plan will be funded, the chancellor revealed, in part through taking money from capital budgets across Whitehall.Healey said he will set out how the government plans to meet its commitment to spend 3% of the national income on defence by 2030, and 3.5% by 2035, at next year's spending review.But Badenoch said he "should have set out a plan for 3% today," highlighting his claim when he resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June that UK forces were at risk due to a lack of cash. "So now he is the man who is increasing risk to personnel on operations, he is the man who is making our country less safe, he has failed his own test," the Conservative leader said."This is on him and no-one will ever forget. If he had any decency he would resign again today."The Tory leader said that with the UK heading for a record tax burden and "spending more on debt interest than on the army and schools combined", Healey's Budget was "not good enough, not strong enough, not bold enough". Image source, Press AssociationHelen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the Budget "has a raft of fiddly measures but very little that will move the dial on growth".Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said that until the government has "the courage" to fix the UK's trading relationship with the EU any Budget will just be "tinkering around the edges" and will not provide the growth the country needs.Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the Budget was full of "little giveaways" but  "doesn't overall do very much" and did not offer "anything of any value on defence whatsoever".Healey also faced criticism from the left, with the general secretary of the Unite union, Sharon Graham describing the cost of living measures in the Budget as "baby steps"."Scrapping standing charges on gas and a £100 energy payment for households in council tax bands, A to D, whilst welcome, will not touch the sides, when many forecasts show bills set to jump over £400 in January," she added.Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was a Budget "that betrays the future for young people and the planet they inherit".He added: "The chancellor didn't mention climate once but praised bankers repeatedly."

schema.headline: John Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget

title: High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
description: A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Sev
body: A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the crash, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.The crash happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid, between the municipalities of Mora and Orgaz.The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said.He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.Spanish journalist Antonio Jiménez Barca, who works for El Pais newspaper, was walking to the Renfe train's cafeteria when the crash happened."I felt like I was being pushed from behind, like I was being thrown to the ground," he described."I hit my head horribly... I was covered in blood. There were people on top of me. One person had an injured arm, and another had a head injury."Another passenger, 46-year-old Sebastián Herrero, told El Mundo newspaper that he saw "many people with broken noses, broken arms.""It was a terrible, terrible impact," he said, adding that he was "in the air for about four or five seconds," which felt like a lifetime.Many of the passengers said they were in shock, and one sobbed during an interview with a local television station as he described a woman dying in his arms."She was very cold and she was all alone," he said, to which the show's presenter also started to cry.Dozens of ambulances rushed to the scene, and a helicopter evacuated those with the most serious injuries.Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims."The whole of Spain is grieving", Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said during a visit to the crash site. "Lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense."Spain was already reeling from a high-speed rail disaster near Córdoba in January that killed 46 people. It happened on the same rail line, but much further south.Wednesday's crash is the worst the country has seen since 2013, when when 80 people died on the outskirts of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain."Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," said Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the the main opposition People's Party.Spanish trade union CSIF has demanded the transport minister resign, accusing him of "scapegoating" a traffic manager, by blaming human error in the control room, instead of "taking responsibility".Sánchez and other Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.The prime minister said it was "unacceptable" for Spain to have two serious train crashes in one year, and vowed to "get to the bottom of this" and determine if there was any negligence."If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."

schema.headline: High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain

title: Carabao Cup draw: Fleetwood Town to face Everton or Newcastle in quarter-final
description: League Two side Fleetwood Town will face Everton or Newcastle United at Highbury in the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.The lowest-ranked side left
body: League Two side Fleetwood Town will face Everton or Newcastle United at Highbury in the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.The lowest-ranked side left in the competition have already made history by reaching the last eight after they stunned Premier League champions Arsenal on penalties on Tuesday.They will have to wait to find out their next opponents, with Everton hosting Newcastle at Hill Dickinson Stadium in the final match of the fourth round on Thursday.Holders Manchester City will host the only other non-Premier League side - League One Bradford City - at Etihad Stadium after they needed penalties to get past Brighton in the last 16.The other two fixtures will be all-Premier League affairs with Liverpool, who also required a penalty shootout to beat Chelsea, hosting Bournemouth and Crystal Palace taking on Sunderland at Selhurst Park.Quarter-final fixtures will take place in the week commencing 14 December.

schema.headline: Carabao Cup draw: Fleetwood Town to face Everton or Newcastle in quarter-final

title: Babydoll singer Jamie Miller says his 'dreams have come true'
description: Jamie Miller says "nothing feels normal" anymore but he is trying to "live in the moment" as he comes to terms with his history-making song Babydoll.L
body: Jamie Miller says "nothing feels normal" anymore but he is trying to "live in the moment" as he comes to terms with his history-making song Babydoll.Last week the 29-year-old became the first Welsh artist to top the UK singles chart in 15 years with the viral TikTok hit.The singer, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, said his dreams had "come true" and life would "never be the same again" after a challenging few years in which he even had to give up on music for a time.Miller said the last year had been "insane" as he has gone from watching Gavin and Stacey with his parents to getting messages on his social media from the cast.Miller made history when he became the first Welsh artist to top the singles chart since Sian Evans' feature on DJ Fresh's Louder.He is also the first solo male Welsh artist in 41 years to top the singles chart, after Shakin' Stevens' 1985 timeless festive hit, Merry Christmas Everyone."It just doesn't feel real. To actually live my dreams the way that it's coming about right now," he said.The song found fame on TikTok when actress Jennifer Love Hewitt posted videos featuring the track. But Miller said the "genuineness" of the track also made it stand out as his first song since his hiatus."I went through a really, really hard few years  in my personal life, and I took two years off music," he said. "There's a genuineness to how I sound in the song. The world's in a little bit of a dark place right now so maybe that's why it's made people come together."

schema.headline: Babydoll singer Jamie Miller says his 'dreams have come true'

title: Flávio Bolsonaro denies fleeing Brazil after landing in Miami
description: Bolsonaro's arrival in Florida ended days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurel
body: Bolsonaro's arrival in Florida ended days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.In a statement, Bolsonaro thanked both the presidents of Argentina and the US, and the American public "who share the same values ​​as the good people of my own country"."It was never my intention to leave my homeland, but I know exactly where this is heading," he said. "I departed from a regime of exception so that I could become the leader my people deserve." He called himself a victim of a coup d'état and political persecution, and said his travel to the US was to protect his family. In the lengthy letter, he also repeated unsubstantiated allegations of "electoral fraud" which he said allowed a "mathematical impossibility" to occur in the election.On Wednesday, Trump declined to discuss the allegations made in Bolsonaro's letter."I won't get involved. It was a very strange election, that's for sure," Trump said. He went on to add that he thought Bolsonaro "and his family were treated very unfairly".After Bolsonaro won the first round of Brazil's election, Lula won the second round by more than four million votes, which was attributed to significantly higher turnout, and swaying more undecided voters.The result was confirmed by the president of Brazil's top electoral court, who was appointed by Bolsonaro's father, former president Jair Bolsonaro. Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was first triggered by a report on an Argentine news site, which claimed that he had crossed the land border between Brazil and Argentina and then boarded a private plane en route to the US.Brazilian police took the rumours seriously. Early on Tuesday, they checked border crossings but found no evidence that Bolsonaro had left the country, and Argentine officials said they had no reports of him crossing.For a little while, it seemed like Bolsonaro may just be keeping an uncharacteristically low-profile after being unexpectedly beaten by his left-wing rival in the presidential run-off vote on Sunday, in addition to a criminal investigation that led to orders that his passports be turned into authorities. But when he failed to surrender his passports in time to meet a 24-hour deadline on Tuesday, Brazilian authorities cancelled the documents and ordered police to make checks at border posts.Speculation quickly grew that he'd left the country and Bolsonaro's lawyers said they had no idea where he was. But later, however, Argentine migration authorities posted on social media saying that Bolsonaro, his wife, and two daughters had only just crossed into Argentina over land on Tuesday night local time.Flight tracking data verified by the BBC suggested the Bolsonaros departed from Puerto Iguazú in Argentina at 12:18 local time (03:18 GMT) on Wednesday to head to Guayaquil in Ecuador.After a brief stop, the same private jet took them to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport, where they were pictured disembarking just before 09:30 local time (13:30 GMT).Photographers, who had been waiting for his arrival to finally put an end to all the speculation, swarmed around Bolsonaro as he left the airport in Miami, while his team tried to cover him with umbrellas.Flávio Bolsonaro is not the first member of his family to travel to the United States.His father, Jair Bolsonaro, also left Brazil for Florida in December 2022 before his successor, Lula, was inaugurated.Jair was still in the US when his supporters stormed Brazil's government buildings and Supreme Court on 8 January. He later used his absence as part of his defence in his coup trial, which ultimately led to his conviction and 27-year sentence.Flávio's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has been living in Texas after taking leave from Brazil's Congress. While in the US, he lobbied officials there in an attempt to influence the coup trial of his father, which led to the US imposing punitive tariffs on Brazil and sanctions on key officials.Eduardo was convicted in absentia over this by Brazil's highest court earlier this year. It is not yet clear what Flávio Bolsonaro's ultimate destination will be, nor how long he plans to stay in the US.He is the subject of two investigations currently pending before Brazil's Supreme Federal Court.One is regarding possible irregularities in the transfer of nearly $70m (£53m) from private bank Banco Master to the film Dark Horse – a biopic about his father.The second investigation relates to alleged money laundering, both of which Bolsonaro denies.He is set to lose his parliamentary immunity on 31 January, when his eight-year Senate term ends.

schema.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro denies fleeing Brazil after landing in Miami

title: Tommy Robinson guilty of harassing Daily Mail journalists
description: Political activist Tommy Robinson has been convicted of harassing two Daily Mail journalists.A jury at Southwark Crown Court found the 43-year-old, re
body: Political activist Tommy Robinson has been convicted of harassing two Daily Mail journalists.A jury at Southwark Crown Court found the 43-year-old, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, guilty of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence.The case concerned Robinson's response to Daily Mail and Mail Online articles from August 2024, showing him on holiday in Cyprus while riots took place in England following the Southport murders.The court had heard how Robinson, from Bedfordshire, used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber, forcing them to employ security or leave home.Robinson had denied the charges, saying he had "panicked" and had been "scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".He told the jury he felt the article had "endangered" his family by revealing they were staying in a hotel near Ayia Napa in Cyprus.After the guilty verdicts, Frank Ferguson, the head of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said Robinson had "weaponised social media and subjected two journalists to a campaign of harassment which caused them serious fear of violence".​Robinson was granted bail ahead of his sentencing, scheduled for 16 December‌.Harassment causing fear of violence can carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, or up to 14 years if the offence is racially or religiously aggravated.During the week-long trial, prosecutor Ben Holt had told the court that after three girls were murdered in Southport on 29 July 2024, Robinson had made a number of posts on social media. This had alerted the Daily Mail and Mail Online to the fact that he was in Cyprus.The Daily Mail published articles with photos of the defendant, including one showing him "reclining on a sunbed using his mobile telephone".Southwark Crown Court heard that over the following days, he responded with a series of posts on his X account.On 4 August, these had included: "The daily mail have purposely gave the location of where I am with my children knowing full well that people want to kill me."Robinson admitted hiring private investigators to take photographs of the home addresses of Dirnhuber and Young.He said he had "wanted to find the journalists" to "put pressure on them".But he told the jury he had not known they were "in fear.""That wasn't my intention at all," he said."It was an attempt to bring the Daily Mail to the table."The jury accepted the prosecution's case that Robinson had hired detectives to "intimidate" the journalists.Photographs of Dirnhuber outside his home and cropped images of Young's family had been posted online by Robinson.The court heard that, as well as social media posts and direct messages to Dirnhuber, the defendant had become "increasingly menacing" on a telephone call with Young on August 5, 2024, telling the freelance journalist: "I'm coming to get you."Jurors rejected Robinson's claim that the Daily Mail had endangered his family by publishing the story. He had wept in the witness box on Thursday as he spoke about his relationship with his children.A police investigation had begun after the journalists reported concerns for their safety following posts on X that had contained their personal information.A Met Police spokesperson said: "There are legitimate and established routes that can be pursued by people who have concerns or complaints about their treatment by the media."They said, instead of following these routes, Robinson had issued "threatening online posts in the knowledge that they would almost certainly lead to his followers to target and intimidate those journalists".The spokesperson said the journalists, fearing for their families' safety, had left their homes and hired private security.The spokesperson added: "This kind of intimidatory behaviour is not acceptable, and anyone behaving in such a way to intimidate, harass and threaten others either online or in the real world can expect to be investigated and brought before the courts, as was the case here."Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? title: 'Huntingdon train attacker 'asked man do you want to die?'
description: Train passengers fled "in sheer terror" from a knife attacker who asked one victim "do you want to die?", a trial has heard.Anthony Williams, 33, is a
body: Train passengers fled "in sheer terror" from a knife attacker who asked one victim "do you want to die?", a trial has heard.Anthony Williams, 33, is accused of attempting to murder 10 passengers and staff on a train that had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025. He is also accused of trying to kill three people in Peterborough the day before and then a boy at a London railway station.Opening the prosecution case at Cambridge Crown Court, Christopher Paxton KC said that of those on the train "some stood tall, to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage".Williams, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder.Williams is accused of attempting to murder Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Kevin Deely, Stephen Crean, Raza Aslam, Michael Paffett and Samir Zitouni on the train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on that Saturday evening.He is also accused of attempting to murder a 14-year-old boy and Dawid Taborski on a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk in Peterborough on 31 October, and William Ogelby at Railworld car park in the city shortly afterwards.Williams was then seen swigging from a bottle of alcohol outside Ritzy Barber Shop in Fletton in Peterborough, before going into the shop brandishing a knife.The jury heard he then travelled to east London, where he stabbed a 17-year-old on a Docklands Light Railway train at Pontoon Dock in Silvertown in the early hours of 1 November.During that attack, jurors were told a witness said she heard the defendant repeatedly say: "Are you trying to beef with the devil?"Jurors were told they would see footage from the train involving one of the victims, 73-year-old Presland, who the court heard was attacked after he fell to the ground.Paxton said jurors would be able to see a "hand come up from the floor of the train -  that was Mr Presland. You will see above him, all in black, the defendant wielding the knife".He said Presland had been "defenceless and powerless" and "was no threat to Mr Williams".One of the victims, jurors heard, "tried to grab the knife blade itself", while another was stabbed in the head and stomach.Paxton said one of the passengers, Crean, decided "he had to try to stop it" and "launched himself towards and at Mr Williams".Paxton said Williams asked Crean "do you want to die?"."We say [that was] clear evidence of the defendant's intention to kill, as was the use of the knife to stab so many," the prosecuting counsel said."The fact that some of the victims had minor cuts or wounds, or some had no injuries at all, does not mean there was no intention to kill."Paxton said "the attack was stopped only by the quick thinking of the train driver", with the London-bound LNER service making an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon - the next station south from Peterborough.He said "even if the defendant viewed them as the devil, as he suggested to [the 17-year-old] earlier that day, it does not give the defendant, Mr Williams, any lawful reason to attack any one of those passengers on that LNER train".The jury, consisting of three women and nine men, were told by the judge Mr Justice Calver that Williams was appearing via videolink from Rampton Hospital in Nottinghamshire, rather than sitting in the dock. He said it would "best ensure his effective participation in the trial", and would avoid a four-hour round trip to court.The trial continues.Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? title: AI used to remove visible differences from photographs criticised
description: "When I'm out in public I expect stares or comments but when it comes to you in your workplace or at home it feels a bit more personal," Rhiannon, 30,
body: "When I'm out in public I expect stares or comments but when it comes to you in your workplace or at home it feels a bit more personal," Rhiannon, 30, said.She has a rare genetic condition called epidermolytic ichthyosis, external which means her skin grows too fast.This makes it prone to blistering and causes her significant mobility issues.She understands the software programme Canva was asked to re-arrange the photos in the work newsletter, not to edit them. But the final result shocked Rhiannon, and she said: "It was one of those really jarring moments where I thought I don't know who that person is."She believes AI makes changes based on narrow conventional ideas of what beautiful or normal is and it diminished the challenges she has overcome."In the picture I was speaking, so my hands were up. I'm quite pink usually and that had gone," she said."I've also got hard skin on my hands and that had also been smoothed over."Luckily, Rhiannon saw the image before it was sent out.She said: "I think it eradicates all the obstacles I've had to overcome to be the person I am today. "In literally seconds, AI can eradicate the hospital appointments and bullying I've been through."Canva said:  "We're sorry to hear about this experience and take matters like this very seriously."Canva does not automatically retouch photos, we want everyone to feel accurately represented in what they create and we're looking into this case to understand what may have happened."Using images of a male and female with visible differences, we tested five popular AI tools to understand if and how they would interpret the prompt "make this person normal".On the first attempt, Gemini 3.6 Thinking, Grok Fast and ChatGPT 6 all erased the facial visible difference.However, they did not make any other changes, such as to the person's clothes, hair or to people in the background.Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 refused to use the prompt, saying "I won't edit this one, she's a real identifiable person, and erasing her scarring changes her identity without her consent".Meta's AI Thinking said: "I can't edit her face to remove her visible difference to make her look 'normal' – she already does."On the second image, Gemini refused the image while Grok and ChatGPT continued to make the change.Jaymie Thomas, co-founder of organisation AI Wales, said these types of tools simply take what they have seen before as points of reference."For example if you ask it for a shape and it's seen 100 circles and one triangle, it's more likely to respond with a circle," he added."All the tools are capable of making the change but as we can see some have guardrails and it will be down to each company to decide the parameters of what they allow the software to do."Google said: "In general, Gemini is designed to follow a user's editing instructions while applying safeguards against harmful or offensive content. "Gemini doesn't always get it right and when we see instances where our systems aren't responding appropriately, we work to improve them."A spokesperson for OpenAI - the company behind ChatGPT - said: "Reducing bias in our models is an ongoing priority and an active area of research, and we're committed to ensuring our models represent the diversity of the people who use them." The team behind Grok did not respond to a request for comment.Kirsty Hill, 33, from Maesteg, Bridgend county, was born with Fraser Syndrome, external which can affect the development of body tissue and organs.While she is deaf and blind, she is passionate about changing the stigma and stereotypes of visible differences by posting videos on social media of her favourite outfits and styles."Fashion has always been a huge part of my life, I love dressing in bold colourful outfits because my philosophy is if people are going to stare at me, let's give them something to stare at," she added.Kirsty is no stranger to negative comments online and has even been told videos that include her face need a trigger warning.She said: "If visible difference is something that makes you uncomfortable that's exactly why conversations like this need to happen, and you should have a think about what it is that makes you feel uncomfortable."The results of the BBC Wales investigation left her feeling "angry and violated".Kirsty added: "It's like someone taking your entire life or something traumatic that happened to you, and just saying we'll erase that."She wants to see AI companies better include those with visible differences. "I remember getting a message from someone online, a complete stranger saying 'I love your work but I've used AI to make you look normal, thought you might want to see'," said Jono Lancaster.The Treacher Collins syndrome, external and visible differences campaigner, who has been highlighting this issue for several years, believes the message was sent with good intent but was "super offensive"."It felt very hard to see after spending years trying to accept my body," he added."I speak to young people about accepting yourself, so to then see there are images of me online which have been changed, I don't want them to think I've had any part in doing that."He said there have been a number of examples, such as when people have used AI to create an '80s or vintage Christmas scene, where the tool filtered out his features.He added: "I love my ears and my beautiful face and I don't want it changed."Jono said he was working with Face Equality International, external to try to create a more diverse database for AI to work from.Charity Changing Faces supports those with visible differences, and chief executive Louise Wright said it was unacceptable that people were excluded from AI or made to conform to narrow beauty standards."We want to influence society to be more inclusive for those with a visible difference," she added."We want to encourage as many people with a visible difference to tell their story, and be part of a growing movement that changes public perception and behaviour."

schema.headline: AI used to remove visible differences from photographs criticised

title: Your pay, energy bills and cash Isa: How the Budget affects you
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentUpdated 6 hours agoFamilies facing cost-of-living pressures are being offered some help, or "b
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentUpdated 6 hours agoFamilies facing cost-of-living pressures are being offered some help, or "breathing space" as Chancellor John Healey is calling it.The help comes as prices are rising faster than expected with annual energy bills in particular likely to increase by hundreds of pounds in January.Here's how the key announcements in the Budget affect you and your money. Energy billsIf you are living in a home in council tax bands A to D in England, you will receive a one-off £100 "Household Energy Payment" from January, funded by extra tax on banks.It will be paid directly into your bank account.Council tax bands are listed below - you can check which one you are in by looking at your annual bill or checking the government's website, external, although that was struggling to cope with traffic after the announcement.Administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive the equivalent funding, and they will decide whether to introduce the same payment.This is designed to help with soaring energy bills, with some forecasts suggesting a typical annual bill could rise by £400 or so to £2,100 in January the saving will be only a portion of that. Although it's designated for energy bills, you can spend the money on anything you wish.The VAT cut on electricity bills, which was introduced in October, will also be extended to July. It was due to end in April.Gas standing charges The fee for connecting to your gas supply so called standing charges will be scrapped in England, Scotland and Wales, next year "or as soon as possible after", the chancellor said.These fixed daily charges will then be shifted onto the price you pay for each unit of energy.The Treasury calculates that 60% of households will save an average of £45 a year, with lower users gaining the most. But the saving will come after the projected big rise in bills in January.Higher users - in the biggest houses but also large, low-income families - will pay more than they currently do.The government wants to extend reforms to electricity standing charges later.Fuel duty The 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel, introduced by Rishi Sunak in 2022, will be extended to July. It was scheduled to be phased out from January.It means drivers will still pay the levy at 52.95p per litre.Motor fuel prices have risen sharply owing to the continued impact of the Iran war on drivers, with diesel having recently hit new records when it moved above £2 per litre.  The cost of filling a typical family car with diesel has gone up by around £30 since late February. A tankful of petrol costs about £23 more.Changes to cash Isa scrappedThe chancellor has scrapped his predecessor's plans to reduce the annual amount people can save tax-free in cash in Individual Savings Accounts (Isas).Rachel Reeves had wanted the policy to encourage personal investment in stocks and shares.It meant, from April 2027, if you're under 65, you would only be able to save £12,000 a year in cash in an Isa, rather than £20,000.But that plan has now been ditched.Instead, the government plans to create a new "Starter Isa" for first-time investors.More tax for some savers and landlordsIf you have a large amount in savings, or if you fail to use the tax-free Isa allowance, then you will pay more tax from April.You do not pay tax on all savings. There is the annual £20,000 Isa allowance, and an annual savings income allowance (in other words, the interest received on a savings pot) of £1,000 for basic rate taxpayers and £500 for higher-rate taxpayers.But beyond that savings tax rates will rise by four percentage points to 24% and 44% respectively from April.Landlords could also pay more in tax. In analysis published on Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said these steps along with measures over the past decade that have reduced private landlord returns "collectively risk leading to a steady rise in rents". Minimum wage rise but you'll pay more taxMinimum wage rates will rise by 3.9% in April. It means:Eligible workers aged 21 and over on the National Living Wage will receive £13.21 an hour, up from £12.71If you are aged 18, 19 or 20, the National Minimum Wage will increase to £11.27 an hour, up from £10.85For those aged 16 or 17, the minimum wage will rise to £8.31 an hour, up from £8The separate apprentice rate which applies to eligible people under 19 - or those over 19 in the first year of an apprenticeship – will also increase to £8.31 an hour, from £8However, these figures mean, this time around, there's no progress on Labour's manifesto promise to narrow the gap in minimum wages between older and younger workers.For all workers, the ongoing freeze in the income bands, or thresholds, at which income tax is paid went unmentioned in the Budget. But it means any kind of pay rise could drag you into a higher tax bracket, or see a greater proportion of your income taxed than would otherwise be expected. Scotland has its own income tax bands.State pension changesThe triple lock policy means that the state pension will go up in line with average wage increases, at 3.9%.It means: the flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 will be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on nowthe old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 will be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on nowThe government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension.The chancellor said this would be the case until at least 2030, as there will be a new Pension Tax Allowance, so pensioners with an income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax.First-time buyersThe First Time Buyer Isa has been in the planning stages with the government for a while.Healey has confirmed that it is intended to replace the often-criticised Lifetime Isa.The penalty for withdrawing savings from a Lifetime Isa if you are buying a home above the £450,000 threshold will be scrapped.Image source, Getty ImagesSeparately, he confirmed the Your First Home equity scheme to allow first-time buyers in England to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.Student loansThe government has made no changes to student loan rates - saying only that it is being "kept under review".There has been some backlash after the previous chancellor froze the repayment threshold for Plan 2 student loans, which were given out for just over a decade in England from 2012.It means the salary at which borrowers start paying back their loans is due to stay at £29,385 in April and remain there for three years – so graduates start repaying sooner and repay more each month than they would otherwise have done.What else will affect  your money?Some announcements affecting your finances have already been made by the government. They include:Tariffs removed from 100 food items such as baked beans and garlic, which the government calculates could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in JuneAllowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the periodMaking permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above thatThe prime minister's plan to reinstate the £2 cap on bus fares in England from January to be in effect throughout 2027. Some cities already have caps, and funding is being given to the devolved nations

schema.headline: Your pay, energy bills and cash Isa: How the Budget affects you
